doc.title: Jason Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Living through the aftermath
summary: They stayed four months in Jackson and about a year in New York before returning to the repaired house. He reflects on staying spiritually steady.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: We were in Jackson for about four months. Eventually we went to New York and went there for about a year. Then – but during that time we were in and out of New Orleans, seeing about the place. After about a year we were able to come back to New Orleans and live in the house that we live in now. But I think spiritually it was – I got through it, but it was something that was a bit overwhelming. It’s something that – I see it for what it is, and I don’t get too depressed thinking about it, but at the same time, I do have a proper perspective on it. It was something that – it was very draining in some ways. But I try not to get too – I don’t let it put me down too much, because at the end of the day, there’s still work you got to do. You still got to – there’s still people that’s going to call me, that want to play on something or want to do this. While I had put it in proper perspective, and while I had to do that, at the same time, you still have to keep moving forward. So I think that, spiritually, that is something that the city still managed to get through. There’s still problems. There’s still things to be worked on. But the city just went through it. They just kept going, like, we’re going to get through it. We’ll come back. We’ll still deal with it.
